procedural_history.originating_court: Special Tribunal (located at Lahore, constituted by Ordinance No. 29 of 1943)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 21, 1962, of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 478 and 479, and 41, 176, 478 and 479 of 1949.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Special Tribunal convicted the appellant on all ten charges. On appeal, the Punjab High Court upheld the conviction in respect of part of charge No. 21, charge No. 22, and charge No. 26, but acquitted him of the rest. The High Court also dealt with issues regarding the examination of witnesses in Burma and Pakistan, and the provision of funds for the appellant's defense.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed two appeals (Nos. 150 & 151/1962) in the Supreme Court against the High Court's upholding of his conviction on part of charge No. 21, charge No. 22, and charge No. 26. The State filed four appeals (Nos. 196 to 199 of 1962) against the High Court's orders of acquittal.

directions: The compulsory fine imposed on the appellant in respect of charge No. 21 which was the subject-matter of Criminal Appeal No. 478 of 1949 in the High Court is reduced from Rs. 1,08,400/· to Rs. 54,200/-.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant was wrongly convicted of the offence of cheating.

facts: The appellant was convicted on three charges of cheating under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code for obtaining money from the Government of Burma by submitting bogus claims for works not carried out and materials not supplied.
The appellant raised two main arguments to challenge his conviction.

First, he argued that the government did not pay him based on his claims, but rather based on the verification reports submitted by its own officers. Therefore, if any cheating occurred, it was committed by those officers, not him.

Second, he argued that he had left Burma on April 5, 1942, while many of the bogus claims related to work allegedly done after that date, so he could not have had personal knowledge that the claims were false.
law: The offence of cheating under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code requires a false representation that deceives a person into delivering property.
The element of knowledge, being a state of mind, does not require direct evidence and can be inferred from the circumstances of the case.
application: The Court rejected the appellant's first argument that the officers' verification broke the chain of causation. It reasoned that the entire process, from the submission of the bogus claims to the final payment, was one continuous transaction initiated by the appellant. The fact that the victim takes steps to verify a false claim before parting with property does not absolve the person who made the initial false representation.

The Court also rejected the appellant's second argument regarding his lack of personal knowledge. It held that the prosecution was not required to provide direct evidence of the appellant's state of mind. The Court stated that the very fact that the claims were found to be bogus and contrary to the facts leads to a strong inference that the appellant knew his representations were false when he made them. The Court further noted that the appellant failed to offer any explanation, such as being misled by someone else, which strengthened the inference of his guilty knowledge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was not wrongly convicted. It found that his submission of bogus claims was the cause of the payment and that his knowledge of the claims' falsity could be properly inferred from the circumstances. Therefore, the conviction for cheating was fully justified.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Tribunal was incompetent to hold the trials because the ordinance under which it was constituted had expired after six months, rendering subsequent extensions invalid.

facts: The appellant challenged the validity of the trials, arguing that the Special Tribunal was incompetent.
The argument was that the Tribunal was constituted under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943, which was issued under s. 72 of the Government of India Act, 1935.
Section 72 stipulated that such an ordinance could only remain in force for a maximum of six months.
Based on this, the appellant claimed the ordinance expired six months after its promulgation on September 9, 1943, making the Tribunal defunct and rendering subsequent extensions invalid.
law: The court identified that the appellant's argument ignored a crucial piece of legislation: s. 1(3) of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940.
This Act suspended the operation of the six-month time limit clause contained in s. 72 of the Government of India Act, 1935.

The court also cited a Federal Court precedent, *J. K. Gas Plant Manufacturing Co. v. The King Emperor*, which had already ruled that this specific Ordinance (No. 29 of 1943) remained valid until September 30, 1946, due to the Emergency Provisions Act.
application: Because the six-month limit was suspended by the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, Ordinance No. 29 of 1943 did not expire in early 1944 as the appellant claimed.
The Tribunal, therefore, functioned competently under this ordinance until its actual expiration date of September 30, 1946.
The court noted that on the very next day, October 1, 1946, the Punjab Ordinance III of 1946 came into force, seamlessly continuing the Tribunal's powers.
This was later replaced by Punjab Act X of 1950, ensuring the Tribunal's authority continued without interruption.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that it was based on a misapprehension of the law. The six-month limit on the original ordinance had been suspended by the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940. Therefore, the Special Tribunal was validly constituted and functioned competently throughout the trials, with its authority being continuously maintained by subsequent ordinances and acts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Tribunal was improperly constituted due to changes in its membership over time.

facts: The Special Tribunal was originally constituted by the Central Government with three members under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943.
Subsequently, one member died and the President of the Tribunal left India, reducing its membership to one.
The Punjab Government then appointed two new members to fill the vacancies.
Later, the law was changed by Punjab Act X of 1950, which reduced the required composition of the Tribunal from three members to one.
law: Under Ordinance No. 29 of 1943, the power to constitute the Tribunal was vested in the Central Government.

Punjab Ordinance III of 1946 continued the Tribunal and, under its section 3(3), gave the Punjab Government the power to "supersede or modify" notifications that had been issued by the Central Government.
Punjab Act X of 1950 altered the law to require the Tribunal to be composed of only one member.
application: The appellant argued that the Punjab Government had no authority to appoint new members, as the power to constitute the Tribunal was never transferred to it from the Central Government.
The Court rejected this argument, reasoning that the appointment of new members was a "modification" of the original notification that constituted the Tribunal.
The Court found that this power to modify was explicitly granted to the Punjab Government under section 3(3) of the Punjab Ordinance.

The Court also noted that during the period when the Tribunal had only one member (while the law required three), no proceedings were taken in the appellant's trial. The trial only resumed after the two new members were appointed.
Furthermore, when the Tribunal later functioned with a single member, it was legally valid because Punjab Act X of 1950 had by then changed the legal requirement for the Tribunal's composition.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Tribunal was properly constituted at each stage. The Punjab Government acted within its legal authority when it appointed new members, and the changes in the Tribunal's composition were either legally sanctioned by new legislation or occurred during periods when no trial proceedings were conducted. Therefore, the Tribunal functioned competently throughout.

issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated by the failure of the authorities to provide adequate funds from the appellant's attached property for his defence.

facts: The appellant's properties and funds were attached under Ordinance 38 of 1944.
The Ordinance required the District Judge to provide reasonably necessary sums from the attached property for the appellant's defense.
The District Judge directed a payment of Rs. 3,000 for the purpose of examining witnesses in Burma, in addition to other payments for maintenance.
A High Court bench reviewed this issue and found on August 23, 1954, that the Rs. 3,000 had been paid and that the attached funds were completely exhausted, leaving no further money available.
The appellant ultimately withdrew his request to examine the witnesses in Burma.
law: Ordinance 38 of 1944, s. 9, provides that a District Judge shall provide, from an applicant's attached property, such sums as may be reasonably necessary for expenses connected with their defense in criminal proceedings.
application: The Court relied on the findings of the High Court, which had previously examined the issue.

The High Court had determined that the funds available from the appellant's attached property were completely exhausted after payments for maintenance and a Rs. 3,000 payment for defense expenses were made.
Since no further funds were available from the attached property, the Court reasoned that there was no refusal by the authorities to provide funds to which the appellant was entitled.

Additionally, the Court found the entire grievance to be immaterial because the appellant himself ultimately withdrew his request to examine the witnesses in Burma, which was the reason for the funding request in the first place.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the trial was not vitiated. The authorities had provided the funds that were available from the appellant's attached property until they were exhausted, and therefore had not wrongfully refused payment. The issue was also rendered moot by the appellant's own action of withdrawing his request for the witnesses.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court committed an error of law in acquitting the appellant of certain charges, thereby justifying interference in the State's appeals.

facts: The State of Punjab filed four appeals against the High Court's decision to acquit the appellant of certain charges.
The High Court had acquitted the appellant because it found that the prosecution had "failed to prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the claims paid to the appellant were bogus."
law: The Supreme Court will only interfere with a High Court's findings of fact if an error of law has been committed.
application: The counsel for the State was unable to show the Supreme Court that the High Court had committed any error of law when it recorded its findings of fact.
The High Court's conclusion that the prosecution failed to meet its burden of proof was a finding of fact.
reasoning.conclusion: Since the State could not demonstrate any error of law in the High Court's decision, the Supreme Court held that the findings of fact recorded by the High Court did not call for any interference and rejected the State's appeals.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant was wrongly convicted of the offence of cheating.
appellant_arguments: The payments made by the government were not a result of the false representations in the appellant's claims.
The payments were made based on the verification reports submitted by various officers who checked the claims.
Therefore, if any cheating occurred, it was committed by the verifying officers, not the appellant.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's false representations in his bills were the direct cause that induced the government to make the payments.
The verifying officers who approved the bogus bills could be guilty of abetting the appellant, but this does not absolve the appellant of the primary offence of cheating.

cases.case_name: Sarwant Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: The provided text does not state the legal principle for which this case was cited.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An offense under section 420 of the Indian Penal Code is established when a person is induced to deliver property through deception, even if the actual delivery of the property occurs after the person has already made the decision to part with it. The subsequent delivery is part of the same transaction and does not reduce the offense to a lesser charge.
obiter: Diaries that are required to be maintained under official rules are admissible in evidence under section 35 of the Evidence Act as records of official acts.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the appellant was rightfully convicted of cheating because his own false representations in the submitted bills were the ultimate cause that induced the government to part with its money. The fact that verifying officers also made false reports might make them guilty of abetment, but it does not negate the appellant's primary role and guilt in the offence.
legal_tests_applied: In an appeal against an acquittal, the appellate court will not interfere with findings of fact unless the lower court has committed an error of law.
For an offence of cheating, the critical element is whether the accused's false representation induced the victim to part with property, even if other parties were involved in the process.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the verifying officers' reports, rather than the appellant's claims, caused the payments. It held that the appellant's representations were the foundational act that culminated in the government making the payments.
The court found that the officers who verified the bogus bills could be guilty of abetting the appellant, but this did not absolve the appellant of the principal offence of cheating.
why_respondent_won: On the cheating conviction, the State's position was upheld because the court found a direct causal link between the appellant's false claims and the government's payments, stating 'it were those representations by the appellant which ultimately cnlminated in the Government of Burma parting with the money'.

On the State's appeals against acquittal, the original accused (as respondent) won because the State failed to show that the High Court committed any 'error of law' in its findings of fact that the prosecution had not proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt for those specific charges.
